Slides (black — mostly clinical pictures), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from the lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no paediatric surgery chapter. Neck masses, rectal bleeding, perianal abscess and haemangioma are not on the slides but have been asked — they are at the end with added background.

  • Common pediatric surgical problems — abdominal wall defects: inguinal hernia · umbilical hernia · hydrocele · omphalocele · undescended testis · gastroschisis · circumcision.
  • Any groin or scrotal swelling → think inguinal hernia first. The key exam skill is telling hernia from hydrocele, and knowing which conditions resolve on their own and which never do.

1. Inguinal hernia

Inguinal hernias in infants — groin swelling extending into the scrotum

  • Hernia = protrusion/outpouching of an organ or tissue outside its containing wall.
TypePathwayTypical population
IndirectEnters internal ring → travels through inguinal canal → exits external ringAdults and children — predominant type in pediatrics
DirectProtrudes directly through the abdominal wall / inguinal triangleAdults only
FeatureAdult herniaPediatric hernia
CauseAcquired — abdominal wall weakness ± ↑ intra-abdominal pressureCongenital — patent processus vaginalis (PPV)
Why not muscular?—Child is too young to have developed wall weakness
  • Processus vaginalis: the testis descends abdomen → internal ring → inguinal canal → external ring → scrotum, accompanied by the processus vaginalis, which should normally close around/before birth. Persistent patency creates a tract between abdomen and scrotum → indirect inguinal hernia. Contents may include bowel, fat, or gonadal structures.
  • Defect that causes an indirect inguinal hernia in children → patent processus vaginalis. 439
  • Boy with a groin lump extending into the scrotum, positive internal ring occlusion test → indirect inguinal hernia. 436

Presentation & natural history

  • Classic picture: painless, intermittent inguinal/scrotal swelling that enlarges with ↑ intra-abdominal pressure or straining (crying), and may reduce spontaneously when the child relaxes.
  • Inguinal hernia has NO spontaneous resolution — the PPV remains patent. Swelling may temporarily disappear, but the hernia persists and carries a significant complication risk → always requires surgical repair.
  • History of a bulge on crying but nothing on examination, testes descended → refer to the paediatric surgery clinic (a convincing history is enough; it won't resolve). 435 ×2
  • Groin swelling by history, none on exam, but thickened right spermatic cord with a cough impulse → no imaging required — the diagnosis is clinical. 436

Complications

  • Incarceration — hernia cannot be reduced back into the abdomen (incarceration ≈ irreducibility).
  • Obstruction — herniated bowel becomes obstructed.
  • Strangulation — compromised blood supply → ischaemia; progression of an incarcerated hernia with vascular compromise.
  • Presentation of incarceration/obstruction (emergency): pain / excessive crying in infants · vomiting · abdominal distension · failure to pass stool · local swelling · redness + marked tenderness over the hernia.
  • What separates an elective hernia from an emergency → reducibility. 435
  • Known hernia, irreducible for 6 hours, no skin changes → incarcerated inguinal hernia (not strangulated). 439 ×3

Emergency management (incarcerated hernia)

  • NPO, IV fluids, good analgesia, then attempt manual reduction.
  • If it reduces: converts from emergency → elective, but do NOT discharge — keep the child admitted and book surgery for the next available slot.
  • If it does not reduce: immediate surgery — risk of bowel ischaemia.
  • 3-month-old booked for herniotomy, now irritable, poor feeding, persistent swelling for 3 h → trial of hernia reduction under sedation and analgesia. 435 ×8 432 ×6

Timing & operation

  • Uncomplicated pediatric inguinal hernia → elective surgery as soon as reasonably available. Not an immediate emergency, but not left for prolonged observation — it will not resolve and complications can occur.
  • Safety-netting: if surgery must be delayed for scheduling reasons, counsel parents on obstruction/incarceration symptoms and to seek urgent care if they develop.
FeatureAdultsChildren
ProcedureReduction + mesh repair (hernioplasty)Herniotomy — division/ligation of the processus vaginalis / hernial sac
WhyReinforces a weakened abdominal wallNo wall weakness to reinforce — the defect is the congenital PPV
Mesh needed?YesNo
  • 2-month-old with a reducible inguinal hernia → herniotomy as early as possible. 439 ×7
  • Father had mesh repair and wants mesh for his 3-month-old → mesh isn't required — the child needs herniotomy only. 438
  • 2-month-old with bilateral hernias and hydrocele → bilateral hernia repair and evacuation of the hydrocele. 434

2. Hydrocele

Hydroceles — smooth, tense scrotal swellings

  • Hydrocele = fluid accumulation around the testis. In infants it reflects a small patent processus vaginalis — too small for bowel, so only fluid passes — plus immature lymphatic absorption. Absorption improves as the lymphatic system matures.
TypeMechanism
CommunicatingSmall PPV remains connected to the abdominal cavity — fluid communicates with the scrotum
Non-communicatingFluid confined around the testis, no ongoing abdominal communication
  • PPV size rule of thumb: larger PPV → bowel/tissue can enter → inguinal hernia. Smaller PPV → fluid only → hydrocele.
  • 6-month-old, bilateral scrotal swellings, can get above them, transillumination positive — cause → patent processus vaginalis. 438

Natural history & management

  • Resolves spontaneously: most infant hydroceles resolve within 6–12 months, or by up to 2 years. Uncomplicated hydrocele carries essentially no major complication risk → observation, not early surgery. Persistent beyond this window → operation.
  • 6-month-old with bilateral non-communicating hydroceles → hydrocelectomy at 1–2 years if not resolved. 438 ×3

Hydrocele vs inguinal hernia — high-yield exam distinction

TestHydroceleInguinal hernia
TransilluminationUsually transilluminates (fluid-filled)Generally does not
"Get above the swelling"Can get above it — confined to scrotumCannot get above it — continues toward inguinal canal
ReducibilityNot reducible (fluid collection)May be reducible
  • Pitfall: transillumination can mislead — e.g. a 4-year-old with scrotal trauma and a haematoma will not transilluminate, falsely read as "not a hydrocele". Never the sole discriminator.
  • Most important clinical sign: "Can you get above the swelling?" — the most reliable bedside discriminator and a favourite exam question. Can get above → confined to scrotum → hydrocele. Cannot get above → continues into the canal → hernia.

Other scrotal swellings asked

Added explanationVaricocele = dilated pampiniform venous plexus, usually left-sided in adolescents: "bag of worms", dragging ache worse on standing/activity, disappears lying down, does not transilluminate, and you can get above it.
  • 15-year-old, left scrotal swelling with dragging pain on activity, disappears supine, transillumination negative, can get above it → varicocele. 437 ×4
Added explanationIn an adult, a new tense scrotal swelling must have a scrotal ultrasound first — a secondary hydrocele can hide a testicular tumour (or epididymo-orchitis) — before any aspiration or repair.
  • 24-year-old, painful scrotal swelling for 1 month, tense swollen right testicle → first step ultrasonography. 437 ×2

3. Undescended testis (cryptorchidism)

Unilateral undescended testis — empty, poorly developed hemiscrotum

  • Inspection: the affected hemiscrotum may look small/poorly developed — a hypoplastic hemiscrotum. Inspection alone cannot confirm UDT.
  • Palpation is required to find whether the testis is present and where along the descent pathway: abdomen → inguinal canal/groin → near scrotum. If not palpable → consider an intra-abdominal location or an absent/atrophic testis.
Added explanationRetractile testis = a normal testis pulled up by an active cremasteric reflex: it can be brought down into the scrotum and stays there briefly before rising again — no surgery, just follow-up. A true UDT cannot be brought down to the scrotum. An ectopic testis lies off the line of descent (perineum, thigh, pubic area).
  • 6-year-old, testis "sometimes not in the scrotum", easily brought down but moves back up → retractile testis. 441 ×4
  • 1-year-old, left testis in the inguinal region and can't be pulled down → undescended testis. 438

Timing

  • Current approach: observe until about 6 months (spontaneous descent can still occur). Historically waited 1.5–2 years, but if the testis has not descended by ~6–7 months, further descent is unlikely → correct at approximately 6–9 months rather than prolonged waiting.
Doctor: correct at ~6–9 months. Exam options and guidelines (AUA/EAU): orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months (within 18 months at the latest). Same message — when 6–9 months isn't offered, choose 6–12 months; never "wait until puberty".
  • 3-month-old, testis palpable in the inguinal region → best time for orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months. 436 ×6
  • 1-year-old, right testis in the inguinal canal → orchidopexy (he is already past 6 months). 441 ×4
  • Regarding UDT, the true statement → orchiopexy is best done at 6–12 months. 427

Complications if left untreated

  • Infertility / impaired testicular function · testicular torsion (increased risk) · malignancy risk · trauma (superficial in the groin, more exposed).

Palpable vs non-palpable testis

FindingImplication / next step
Palpable (in groin)Location established clinically
Non-palpableIntra-abdominal testis, absent/atrophic testis, or loss after intrauterine torsion. Ultrasound may show nonspecific structures and cannot reliably confirm a true testis.
  • Key rule: diagnostic laparoscopy is the key investigation for a truly non-palpable testis — both diagnostic and therapeutic.
  • UDT felt as a mass in the groin — pre-op imaging → no further radiological imaging is needed. 439 ×2
  • 6-month-old, left testis not palpable → best modality to localize it → diagnostic laparoscopy. 435 ×6

4. Umbilical hernia

Umbilical hernias in children — including a large proboscoid one

FeatureAdultPediatric
CauseAcquired abdominal-wall weakness / ↑ intra-abdominal pressureFailure/delay of normal umbilical ring closure after cord clamping (congenital)
  • The cord is clamped after birth and the area normally closes by scar/fibrous tissue.
  • Resolves spontaneously — the ring closes gradually as scar matures. Incarceration and strangulation are extremely uncommon in children → observe until approximately 4–5 years / preschool age (timing flexible). Persistent hernia at preschool age → operative closure.
  • 5-month-old with a reducible umbilical swelling → surgical repair between 4–5 years if not spontaneously resolved. 438 ×4
  • 5-year-old, umbilical swelling since birth, reducible, 1-cm defect → surgical repair. 439 ×3

Quick timing comparison

ConditionSpontaneous resolution?Management timing
Inguinal herniaNeverElective repair soon after diagnosis
HydroceleUsually, yesObserve; most resolve by 6–12 months, up to 1–2 years if uncomplicated
Undescended testisOnly if earlyObserve to 6 months; correct at ~6–9 months if persistent
Umbilical herniaUsually, yesObserve until ~4–5 years / preschool age

5. Abdominal wall defects

  • Omphalocele · Gastroschisis.
  • Noted by the professor as general awareness rather than a primary exam focus.
DefectDescriptionUrgency
OmphaloceleCongenital abdominal wall defect centred at the umbilical region—
GastroschisisBowel protrudes through the abdominal wall, directly exposed to the atmosphereEmergency — exposed bowel vulnerable to contamination/bacteria
  • Danger point: gastroschisis is more urgent than omphalocele because the exposed bowel has no protective covering.
Added explanationGastroschisis — defect usually right of the umbilical cord, no sac, usually isolated (bowel atresia the main association), young mothers. Omphalocele — central, covered by a sac with the cord inserting into it, may contain liver, and is often associated with other anomalies (cardiac, chromosomal, Beckwith–Wiedemann). At birth for gastroschisis: cover the bowel in a sterile bowel bag/cling film, keep warm, NG tube, IV fluids, urgent surgery.

6. Circumcision

  • Indications · Contraindications · Methods · Complications.
  • A very common procedure, performed by urologists, pediatric surgeons, and other appropriately trained physicians.
  • Indications: religious/cultural reasons (most common) · pathological phimosis (foreskin cannot be retracted due to scarring) · recurrent balanitis/balanoposthitis · recurrent UTI, especially with urinary tract abnormalities · recurrent paraphimosis.
  • High-yield contraindications: 1. Hypospadias — the foreskin may be needed later for surgical repair. 2. Bleeding disorder.
  • Complications: bleeding — most common early complication · infection · pain/swelling · meatal/urethral injury · adhesions/skin bridges.
Added explanationMethods: device techniques (e.g. Plastibell, Gomco clamp) in infants, or a freehand (dorsal-slit / sleeve) excision — older children usually under general anaesthesia.
  • 3-month-old with hypospadias brought for circumcision → don't circumcise — re-evaluate after 6 months (keep the foreskin for the hypospadias repair). 437 ×3

7. Other paediatric questions asked (not on the slides)

Neck masses

Added explanationThyroglossal duct cyst — midline neck mass in a child that moves with swallowing and with tongue protrusion (attached to the hyoid by the tract). Treatment = Sistrunk operation: cyst + tract + central part of the hyoid, which keeps recurrence low.
  • 12-year-old, neck mass moving with swallowing and tongue protrusion → Sistrunk operation. 437 ×3
Added explanationCystic hygroma (macrocystic lymphatic malformation) — soft, compressible, brilliantly transilluminating swelling present at birth, classically in the posterior triangle of the neck. A branchial cyst is different: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid at the junction of its upper and middle thirds, usually seen in young adults, does not transilluminate brightly.
  • Neck swelling at birth, posterior triangle, transilluminates → cystic hygroma. 426

Rectal bleeding & perianal swelling

Added explanationJuvenile polyp — the commonest cause of painless rectal bleeding in toddlers (peak 2–5 years): streaks of bright blood on the stool with a normal anal examination; may prolapse. An anal fissure is the commonest cause in infants but is seen on examination (posterior midline tear) with pain on defecation.
  • 1-year-old, streaks of blood with stool for 2 weeks, normal examination → juvenile polyp. 438
Added explanationPerianal abscess in infants — almost always boys under 1 year; tender red perianal swelling → incision and drainage. Antibiotics alone don't treat an abscess; a fistula-in-ano may follow.
  • 6-month-old, 8-mm tender red perianal swelling for 2 days → incision and drainage with antibiotics for 5–7 days. 434 ×2

Vascular lesions

Added explanationInfantile haemangioma — absent or faint at birth, appears in the first weeks, grows rapidly (proliferative phase, first year), then slowly involutes. A port-wine stain (capillary malformation) is present at birth, flat, and grows with the child; an AV malformation is a fast-flow lesion, usually present at birth and enlarging later.
  • Small raised red lesion on the nose appearing slowly after birth → infantile haemangioma. 438
